summary: HLA-B*57:01 positivity confers high risk of potentially fatal abacavir hypersensitivity reaction.

phenotypes.recommendation: Abacavir may be used per standard dosing.
Do NOT prescribe abacavir; choose an alternative agent.

testing: Mandatory before starting abacavir.

references.label: CPIC Guideline for abacavir and HLA-B

summary: Reduced TPMT or NUDT15 activity markedly increases the risk of life-threatening thiopurine-induced myelosuppression.

phenotypes.recommendation: Standard starting dose.
Reduce starting dose (e.g. 30–80%); titrate to tolerance with monitoring.

phenotypes.implication: Very high risk of severe myelosuppression.
phenotypes.recommendation: Drastically reduce dose or use an alternative immunosuppressant.

testing: Test TPMT and NUDT15 before initiating thiopurines; continue FBC monitoring regardless.

references.label: CPIC Guideline for thiopurines and TPMT/NUDT15

summary: CYP2C19 loss-of-function reduces conversion of clopidogrel to its active metabolite, lowering antiplatelet effect and increasing thrombotic risk (notably after PCI/ACS).

phenotypes.recommendation: Clopidogrel at standard dose.

phenotypes.implication: Reduced active metabolite; possible diminished response.
phenotypes.recommendation: Consider an alternative antiplatelet (e.g. prasugrel or ticagrelor) where appropriate.

phenotypes.implication: Significantly reduced response; higher event risk after PCI/ACS.
phenotypes.recommendation: Use an alternative antiplatelet (prasugrel/ticagrelor) unless contraindicated.

testing: Consider in ACS/PCI where antiplatelet response is critical.

references.label: CPIC Guideline for clopidogrel and CYP2C19

summary: DPYD deficiency impairs fluoropyrimidine catabolism, causing severe (potentially fatal) toxicity — mucositis, myelosuppression, diarrhoea, neurotoxicity.

phenotypes.recommendation: Standard dosing.

phenotypes.implication: Reduced DPD activity; increased toxicity risk.
phenotypes.recommendation: Reduce starting dose (e.g. 50%) and titrate to toxicity/effect.

phenotypes.implication: Very high risk of severe toxicity.
phenotypes.recommendation: Avoid fluoropyrimidines; select an alternative regimen.

testing: DPYD genotyping recommended before fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy in many guidelines.

references.label: CPIC Guideline for fluoropyrimidines and DPYD

drug: Oxidant drugs (primaquine, tafenoquine, dapsone, rasburicase, nitrofurantoin, sulfonamides)
summary: G6PD deficiency predisposes to acute haemolytic anaemia when exposed to oxidant drugs; severity varies with the deficiency class.

phenotypes.recommendation: Oxidant drugs may be used per standard guidance.

phenotypes.implication: High risk of acute haemolysis with oxidant exposure.
phenotypes.recommendation: Avoid oxidant drugs, or use only with explicit dose adjustment and haemolysis monitoring per drug-specific guidance (e.g. primaquine/tafenoquine require documented normal G6PD).

testing: Quantitative G6PD testing before primaquine/tafenoquine and before rasburicase.

references.label: CPIC Guideline for rasburicase and G6PD; WHO malaria guidance on 8-aminoquinolines

summary: HLA-B*15:02 (common in some Southeast/East Asian populations) confers markedly increased risk of carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis.

phenotypes.implication: Lower SJS/TEN risk from this allele.
phenotypes.recommendation: Carbamazepine may be used per standard guidance (HLA-A*31:01 separately modifies risk).
Do NOT use carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine/phenytoin) in carbamazepine-naive patients; choose an alternative.

testing: Screen in at-risk ancestries before starting carbamazepine.

references.label: CPIC Guideline for carbamazepine and HLA-B

summary: CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genotype substantially influence warfarin dose requirements and bleeding risk during initiation.

phenotypes.recommendation: Standard initiation with INR-guided titration.

phenotypes.implication: Lower dose requirement; higher early bleeding risk.
phenotypes.recommendation: Use genotype-guided/lower starting dose where available; intensify INR monitoring.

testing: Optional; genotype-guided dosing algorithms exist but warfarin remains INR-titrated regardless.

references.label: CPIC Guideline for warfarin and CYP2C9/VKORC1

summary: CYP2D6 converts codeine/tramadol to active opioid metabolites. Ultrarapid metabolisers risk life-threatening opioid toxicity; poor metabolisers get inadequate analgesia.

phenotypes.recommendation: Standard dosing.

phenotypes.implication: Excessive active metabolite; risk of respiratory depression (and in breastfeeding, neonatal toxicity).
phenotypes.recommendation: Avoid codeine/tramadol; use an alternative analgesic.
Avoid codeine/tramadol for analgesia; use an alternative.

testing: Consider where opioid response is unexpected; codeine contraindicated in children and breastfeeding regardless.

references.label: CPIC Guideline for codeine and CYP2D6

drug: Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole)
summary: CYP2C19 metaboliser status alters PPI plasma exposure; ultra-rapid metabolisers may fail H. pylori eradication or maintenance acid suppression at standard doses, poor metabolisers may have higher exposure / interactions.

phenotypes.implication: Higher PPI exposure; effective acid suppression at standard doses.
phenotypes.recommendation: Use standard dosing; consider lower dose for very long-term therapy.
Standard dosing.
Standard dosing.

phenotypes.implication: Lower PPI exposure; risk of treatment failure (H. pylori eradication, refractory reflux).
phenotypes.recommendation: Use higher dose or longer course; for H. pylori, prefer a PPI less affected by CYP2C19 (rabeprazole, esomeprazole) or add bismuth quadruple therapy.

testing: Pre-emptive PGx panel includes CYP2C19; reactive testing useful when H. pylori eradication fails or reflux is refractory to standard PPI.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — CYP2C19 and proton pump inhibitor dosing (2020)

drug: SSRIs primarily metabolised by CYP2C19 (citalopram, escitalopram, sertraline)
summary: CYP2C19 phenotype alters exposure of citalopram/escitalopram (and to lesser extent sertraline). Poor metabolisers risk QT prolongation; ultra-rapid metabolisers risk treatment failure.

phenotypes.implication: Markedly increased citalopram/escitalopram exposure; QT prolongation risk.
phenotypes.recommendation: Reduce citalopram/escitalopram dose by 50%; or choose an SSRI not primarily metabolised by CYP2C19 (e.g. fluoxetine, paroxetine — but consider their own pharmacology).
Initiate at standard dose, titrate with awareness of higher exposure.
Standard dosing.

phenotypes.implication: Lower exposure → higher risk of treatment failure for citalopram/escitalopram.
phenotypes.recommendation: Consider alternative SSRI not primarily metabolised by CYP2C19, or higher dose with close monitoring.

testing: Reactive testing after SSRI failure or intolerance; pre-emptive in panel-based PGx.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — CYP2C19 and CYP2D6 with SSRIs (2023 update)

drug: SSRIs metabolised by CYP2D6 (fluoxetine, paroxetine, fluvoxamine partially)
summary: CYP2D6 phenotype alters fluoxetine/paroxetine exposure. Poor metabolisers may have higher exposure and adverse effects; ultra-rapid metabolisers may have treatment failure.

phenotypes.recommendation: Consider 50% dose reduction OR alternative SSRI not primarily CYP2D6-dependent.
Standard dosing.

phenotypes.implication: Lower exposure; higher risk of failure.
phenotypes.recommendation: Consider alternative SSRI; if continuing, titrate to clinical response with awareness of higher dose requirement.

testing: Reactive after poor response/intolerance, or pre-emptive panel.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 with SSRIs (2023 update)

drug: Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine, desipramine, clomipramine, doxepin)
summary: CYP2D6 (and CYP2C19 for tertiary amines) alter TCA exposure. Poor metabolisers risk cardiotoxicity and anticholinergic toxicity; ultra-rapid metabolisers may fail therapy.

phenotypes.implication: Risk of higher TCA / metabolite exposure → anticholinergic, sedation, QT prolongation.
phenotypes.recommendation: Reduce starting dose by 50%; use therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) or choose a non-TCA.
Standard dosing.

phenotypes.implication: Lower exposure → higher risk of treatment failure.
phenotypes.recommendation: Consider alternative; if continuing, TDM is essential.

testing: Useful when TDM unavailable or there has been intolerance / non-response at standard doses.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 with TCAs (2016, updated)

summary: Tamoxifen is bioactivated by CYP2D6 to endoxifen (the active anti-oestrogen). Poor metabolisers and those on strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine, bupropion) generate less endoxifen and may have reduced breast cancer recurrence-free survival.

phenotypes.implication: Substantially lower endoxifen exposure; possibly reduced efficacy.
phenotypes.recommendation: Consider an alternative endocrine therapy (aromatase inhibitor in postmenopausal women); avoid concomitant strong CYP2D6 inhibitors.
Standard dose; avoid CYP2D6 inhibitors; consider higher dose (40 mg) if continuing tamoxifen.
Standard 20 mg daily.

testing: Consider in premenopausal women starting adjuvant tamoxifen; helpful before adding a strong CYP2D6-inhibitor antidepressant.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — CYP2D6 and tamoxifen (2018)

summary: CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolisers have lower ondansetron/tropisetron exposure and higher antiemetic failure for chemotherapy-induced nausea/vomiting.

phenotypes.implication: Lower exposure; antiemetic failure more likely.
phenotypes.recommendation: Select an alternative 5-HT3 antagonist not primarily CYP2D6-cleared (granisetron, palonosetron).
Standard dosing.

testing: Useful in oncology patients with ondansetron failure.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — CYP2D6 and ondansetron/tropisetron (2017)

summary: CYP2D6 poor metabolisers have 5- to 10-fold higher atomoxetine exposure and more adverse effects (sleep disturbance, decreased appetite, cardiovascular).

phenotypes.implication: Markedly higher exposure; more adverse effects.
phenotypes.recommendation: Start at reduced dose (0.5 mg/kg/day) and titrate slowly; review after 4 weeks.
Standard dosing per label.
Titrate to higher dose if needed for response; consider alternative if no benefit.

testing: Helpful pre-treatment in children/adolescents starting atomoxetine.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — CYP2D6 and atomoxetine (2019)

summary: Aripiprazole is metabolised by CYP2D6 and CYP3A4; CYP2D6 poor metabolisers have higher exposure and the label recommends dose reduction.

phenotypes.implication: Higher aripiprazole exposure; more sedation, akathisia.
phenotypes.recommendation: Halve the recommended dose. Also halve when given with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor.
Standard dosing.

testing: Useful in patients with intolerance to low doses.

references.label: FDA label for aripiprazole — CYP2D6 dosing guidance

summary: CYP2D6 poor metabolisers have higher haloperidol exposure and greater risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and QT prolongation.

phenotypes.recommendation: Use lowest effective dose; monitor ECG; consider alternative.
Titrate to response; if no benefit at higher dose, change agent.
Standard dosing.

testing: Helpful in EPS at low doses or treatment failure.

references.label: DPWG (Dutch Pharmacogenetics Working Group) — haloperidol guidance

summary: CYP3A5 expressers (carriers of *1 allele) clear tacrolimus faster and need higher starting doses to reach target trough concentrations after transplant.

phenotypes.implication: Higher clearance; standard doses give sub-therapeutic trough.
phenotypes.recommendation: Start at 1.5–2× the standard mg/kg dose; titrate with TDM to target trough.
Standard mg/kg starting dose; titrate with TDM.

testing: Pre-transplant CYP3A5 genotyping accelerates achievement of target trough and reduces acute rejection in renal transplant.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — CYP3A5 genotype and tacrolimus dosing (2015)

drug: Simvastatin (and to a lesser extent atorvastatin, pravastatin, rosuvastatin)
summary: SLCO1B1 decreased-function variants reduce hepatic uptake of statins (especially simvastatin), raising plasma levels and the risk of myopathy / rhabdomyolysis.

phenotypes.phenotype: Decreased function (one or two T521C alleles)
phenotypes.implication: Higher plasma simvastatin exposure; increased myopathy risk.
phenotypes.recommendation: Avoid simvastatin doses > 20 mg; prefer rosuvastatin, pravastatin, or pitavastatin at standard doses.
Standard dosing per cardiovascular risk.

testing: Useful pre-emptively (panel) or after statin-associated muscle symptoms.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — SLCO1B1, ABCG2, CYP2C9 and statin-associated musculoskeletal symptoms (2022)

summary: UGT1A1 reduced-function variants impair glucuronidation of irinotecan's active metabolite SN-38, causing severe neutropenia and diarrhoea at standard doses.

phenotypes.implication: Markedly increased SN-38 exposure; severe neutropenia / diarrhoea risk.
phenotypes.recommendation: Reduce irinotecan starting dose by ~30% and re-escalate based on tolerance (FDA label); avoid in severe organ dysfunction.
Standard dose with vigilant monitoring; reduce if grade ≥3 toxicity.
Standard dosing per regimen.

testing: Pre-treatment testing recommended in many guidelines for high-dose irinotecan (>180 mg/m²).

references.label: FDA label for irinotecan; DPWG guideline; ESMO recommendation

summary: Atazanavir inhibits UGT1A1, and UGT1A1*28 carriers have elevated bilirubin glucuronidation impairment, resulting in clinically significant hyperbilirubinaemia (jaundice, scleral icterus). Not dangerous but cosmetically distressing.

phenotypes.implication: Very high risk of clinical jaundice.
phenotypes.recommendation: Counsel patient or choose an alternative protease inhibitor / integrase strand transfer inhibitor.
Standard atazanavir use; warn about possible jaundice.

testing: Useful when atazanavir is preferred and patient wants risk estimate.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — UGT1A1 and atazanavir (2015)

summary: HLA-B*58:01 confers >100-fold risk of allopurinol-induced severe cutaneous adverse reaction (SCAR — SJS/TEN, DRESS). Prevalence is high in Han Chinese, Thai, Korean populations.

phenotypes.implication: Very high risk of SJS/TEN/DRESS with allopurinol.
phenotypes.recommendation: Do NOT prescribe allopurinol. Use febuxostat or another urate-lowering therapy.
Standard allopurinol dosing per renal function; start low (50–100 mg) and titrate.

testing: Mandatory before allopurinol initiation in Han Chinese, Korean and Thai patients (American College of Rheumatology, Taiwan FDA).

references.label: CPIC Guideline — HLA-B and allopurinol (2015, updated)

summary: HLA-A*31:01 carriers (more common in Northern European and Japanese populations) have ~10-fold increased risk of carbamazepine hypersensitivity spectrum reactions (maculopapular rash, SJS/TEN, DRESS).

phenotypes.implication: Increased risk of carbamazepine hypersensitivity (any severity).
phenotypes.recommendation: Avoid carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine where possible; choose levetiracetam, lamotrigine (caution titration), or valproate per indication.
Standard use; combine with HLA-B*15:02 testing in Asian patients.

testing: Recommended in patients of European or Japanese ancestry before carbamazepine.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — HLA-A, HLA-B and carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine (2017)

summary: HLA-B*13:01 is strongly associated with dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (DHS, a DRESS-like reaction) in Han Chinese, South-East Asian and some African populations.

phenotypes.implication: High risk of DHS within 4–8 weeks of dapsone start.
phenotypes.recommendation: Avoid dapsone; use alternative therapy for leprosy or PCP prophylaxis (e.g. atovaquone, pentamidine, clofazimine-based regimens).
Standard dapsone use with monitoring during first 8 weeks.

testing: Recommended pre-treatment in Han Chinese and South-East Asian populations; some leprosy programmes test routinely.

references.label: WHO leprosy programme guidance; CPIC informational annotation

summary: CYP2B6 poor metabolisers have 2- to 3-fold higher efavirenz plasma concentrations and more central nervous system adverse effects (vivid dreams, dizziness, depression).

phenotypes.implication: Higher efavirenz exposure; more CNS toxicity.
phenotypes.recommendation: Reduce efavirenz dose to 400 mg/day (or switch to dolutegravir-based regimen).
Consider 400 mg/day if CNS symptoms persist.
Standard 600 mg/day.

phenotypes.implication: Sub-therapeutic exposure; virological failure / resistance risk.
phenotypes.recommendation: Consider alternative ARV regimen.

testing: Useful where efavirenz remains first-line and CNS toxicity is limiting tolerance.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — CYP2B6 and efavirenz (2019)

summary: NAT2 slow acetylators have higher isoniazid exposure and increased risk of hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy; rapid acetylators may be at risk of treatment failure / acquired resistance at standard doses.

phenotypes.implication: Higher exposure; increased hepatotoxicity and neuropathy risk.
phenotypes.recommendation: Use standard dose with pyridoxine 25–50 mg daily; monitor LFTs in first 2 months. Consider dose reduction if intolerance.
Standard dose with pyridoxine prophylaxis as per WHO.
Standard dose; ensure adherence; do not increase dose empirically.

testing: Currently not routine; useful where INH-induced hepatitis recurs or in pharmacokinetic-guided TB regimens.

references.label: WHO TB Programmatic Management of Drug-Resistant TB; CPIC informational annotation

summary: Phenytoin is metabolised by CYP2C9; reduced-function variants raise the risk of toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia, confusion). HLA-B*15:02 confers high risk of SJS/TEN, especially in patients of Han Chinese / South-East Asian descent.

phenotypes.implication: Higher phenytoin exposure; toxicity risk at standard doses.
phenotypes.recommendation: Reduce starting maintenance dose by 25–50%; use therapeutic drug monitoring; adjust to free phenytoin if available.

phenotypes.implication: High risk of SJS/TEN with phenytoin.
phenotypes.recommendation: Do NOT use phenytoin; choose levetiracetam or valproate.
Standard dosing with TDM.

testing: HLA-B*15:02 in Han Chinese / SE Asian patients before phenytoin or carbamazepine.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — CYP2C9 and HLA-B and phenytoin (2014, updated 2020)

variant: Pathogenic variants in RYR1 or CACNA1S
drug: Volatile inhaled anaesthetics (sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane, halothane) and depolarising muscle relaxant suxamethonium (succinylcholine)
summary: Pathogenic RYR1 or CACNA1S variants confer susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia (MH), a life-threatening hypermetabolic crisis triggered by volatile anaesthetics or suxamethonium.

phenotypes.phenotype: MH-susceptible (pathogenic RYR1/CACNA1S variant or prior in vitro contracture test positive)
phenotypes.implication: Risk of fulminant MH on exposure.
phenotypes.recommendation: AVOID all volatile anaesthetics and suxamethonium. Use total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) with propofol and non-depolarising relaxants. Dantrolene must be readily available.
Routine anaesthesia.

testing: Testing indicated in patients with personal/family history of MH or unexplained masseter spasm under anaesthesia.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — RYR1 and CACNA1S and volatile anaesthetics and suxamethonium (2018)

phenotypes.implication: Markedly elevated voriconazole concentrations → hepatotoxicity, visual disturbance, neurotoxicity.
phenotypes.recommendation: AVOID voriconazole in adults if alternative azole available (e.g. isavuconazole, posaconazole). If voriconazole required, start at 50% standard dose with therapeutic drug monitoring (target trough 1–5.5 mg/L).
Use standard dosing with TDM; adjust based on trough levels.
Standard dosing with TDM.

phenotypes.implication: Subtherapeutic concentrations → treatment failure, breakthrough invasive fungal infection.
phenotypes.recommendation: Consider alternative azole (isavuconazole, posaconazole) not metabolised primarily by CYP2C19. If voriconazole used, may require higher doses + close TDM.

testing: Pre-emptive testing recommended in adults before invasive fungal infection prophylaxis or treatment, particularly in haematology / transplant. ALWAYS combine with TDM (essential regardless of genotype — target trough 1–5.5 mg/L).

references.label: CPIC Guideline for CYP2C19 and Voriconazole Therapy (2017, updated).

variant: Gating mutations (G551D, G178R, S549N/R, G1244E, G1349D, S1251N, S1255P) and residual function variants
drug: Ivacaftor (and combination therapies: lumacaftor/ivacaftor, tezacaftor/ivacaftor, elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor)

phenotypes.phenotype: Gating mutation (e.g. G551D) — homozygous or heterozygous with one F508del
phenotypes.recommendation: Ivacaftor monotherapy ≥ 6 months of age. Sweat chloride and pulmonary function improve markedly.
Triple-combination elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta/Kaftrio) — landmark efficacy in this population.

phenotypes.phenotype: Residual function or minimal function mutations
phenotypes.recommendation: Variant-specific — consult FDA / EMA label or CF clinic geneticist. Combination therapies increasingly approved for broader mutation spectrum.
Symptomatic CF therapy; trial enrolment for novel modulators.

testing: CFTR genotype is part of newborn screening confirmation; required before initiating any CFTR modulator. Specific mutation determines which modulator is licensed.

references.label: FDA label — Ivacaftor (Kalydeco), elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta).
Middleton PG et al. Elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor for cystic fibrosis with a single Phe508del allele. NEJM 2019.

drug: Celecoxib, ibuprofen, flurbiprofen, lornoxicam, meloxicam, piroxicam, tenoxicam (CYP2C9-substrate NSAIDs)

phenotypes.implication: Substantially elevated NSAID exposure → increased GI bleeding, AKI, hypertension.
phenotypes.recommendation: AVOID CYP2C9-substrate NSAIDs OR start at 25–50% standard dose with close monitoring (GI symptoms, BP, renal function, platelet count). Prefer non-CYP2C9 NSAIDs (paracetamol, topical NSAID) if available.
Start at lower end of dose range; titrate to effect with usual GI / renal monitoring.
Standard dosing.

variant: CYP2D6 phenotype (PM, IM, NM, RM, UM)

phenotypes.implication: Reduced conversion of oxycodone to oxymorphone, hydrocodone to hydromorphone — may have REDUCED analgesia compared with normal metabolisers. Less clinically obvious than the codeine PM issue, because parent compound retains intrinsic activity.
phenotypes.recommendation: Standard initial dose; if inadequate analgesia despite titration, consider non-CYP2D6 opioid (morphine, hydromorphone, fentanyl, methadone, buprenorphine).
Standard dosing.

references.label: CPIC Guideline for CYP2D6, OPRM1, and COMT genotypes and select opioids (2021).

variant: CYP2D6 phenotype (PM, IM, NM, RM, UM)
drug: Metoprolol (and other CYP2D6-metabolised beta-blockers: carvedilol partially, propafenone)

phenotypes.implication: Up to 5-fold higher metoprolol exposure → bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue.
phenotypes.recommendation: Start metoprolol at 25% standard dose and titrate slowly with vital-sign monitoring. Alternative: bisoprolol (not CYP2D6-metabolised) for chronic use.
Start at 50–75% standard dose; usual titration.
Standard dosing.
Consider alternative (bisoprolol, atenolol) not dependent on CYP2D6. If metoprolol used, higher doses may be needed.

variant: CYP3A5 *3 (loss-of-function; high frequency in non-African ancestry); *1 (functional)

Standard dosing.

Standard dosing.

Standard dosing.

testing: Useful with prior statin-associated muscle symptoms.

references.label: CPIC Guideline — SLCO1B1, ABCG2, CYP2C9 and statin-associated musculoskeletal symptoms (2022)

summary: CYP2D6 metaboliser status influences Risperidone exposure and tolerability; dosing adjustments reduce adverse events.

phenotypes.implication: Reduced Venlafaxine exposure or accelerated active metabolite formation.

summary: CYP2D6 metaboliser status influences Fluvoxamine exposure and tolerability; dosing adjustments reduce adverse events.

phenotypes.implication: Markedly increased Fluvoxamine exposure; raised ADR risk.

Consider 25–50% dose reduction; titrate to clinical response.
